evidence: GPT-5 (high reasoning, with web search + code interpreter) generated GDPval deliverables (PDFs, PPTX, etc.) and submitted them without rendering or visually inspecting them: only 15% of runs used the model's multimodal capability to look at the artifact it had just produced. Consequently >50% of PDFs shipped with black-square artifacts and 86% of PPTX files had egregious formatting defects (cut-off text, overlapping/blank elements). The rendered output was trivially viewable inside the local container — the agent simply did not look. Adding a prompt that forced the agent to convert deliverables to PNGs and inspect them lifted self-inspection from 15% → 97% and eliminated PDF artifacts, confirming the signal was in the observation space all along.
reasoning: Checked Note 3 (Observation Failure vs Reasoning Failure): the model was capable — when asked to look, it could and did diagnose the defects — so the root is not a reasoning incapacity but a failure to consult an available local signal. Checked Note 11 (Satisficing): plausible alternative, since the agent stopped early before verifying. But satisficing is about deliberate effort minimization against a satisfiable spec; here at high reasoning effort the agent spent ample effort generating content, just never looked at its own output — closer to overlooking an available cue than to cutting corners. Checked Note 8 (Instruction-Grader Mismatch): the original prompt didn't mandate visual inspection, but graders judged the actual artifact quality, which is the legitimate deliverable spec, not a hidden criterion. Tool, memory, context-compaction, subagent, and external-service notes do not apply. The rendered file sat in the local environment unobserved — env (local) — model / Observation Failure is the precise locus.

I have read GDPval Section 3.4 ("Increasing Reasoning Effort and Scaffolding") and Appendix A.3 ("Additional Detail on Prompt-Tuning"), plus the surrounding Section 3.3 ("Model Strengths and Weaknesses") that motivates them. The cited material describes the *aggregate behaviour pattern* of GPT-5 (high reasoning effort, custom harness with web search + code interpreter) across the GDPval gold subset (220 tasks), not a single named trajectory. Here is a chronological, observation-only account of what is reported.

# Chronological account of the GPT-5 (high reasoning) agent's behaviour on GDPval

## 1. Task and setup
- The agent was given GDPval gold-subset prompts: real-world, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks contributed by industry experts across 9 sectors and 44 occupations. Each prompt typically includes a written request plus up to 17 reference files (spreadsheets, slide decks, PDFs, images, audio, video, CAD, etc.) and asks for a deliverable file (often PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, or ZIP). Average expert completion time is ~7 hours; some tasks span weeks.
- The agent was GPT-5 at *high* reasoning effort, running in OpenAI's custom GDPval harness with the **web search** and **code interpreter** tools enabled, in background-sampling mode. Several non-default libraries were preinstalled in the container. Each prompt was sampled three times for the headline run.

## 2. Steps and tool calls observed in the baseline (pre-mitigation) runs
The paper reports the following observable behaviours of the unprompted agent across the gold subset (Section 3.3 and the opening of Section 3.4):

- The agent read the prompt + reference files, used web search and code interpreter, and then generated deliverable files (PDFs, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, etc.) inside the container.
- For multimodal deliverables, the agent typically **did not** use its multi-modal capabilities to render or inspect what it had just produced before submitting. The paper reports the rate of agents "using their multi-modal capabilities to inspect deliverables" at only **15%** prior to the prompt change.
- Stylistic tells noted by graders: outputs "often used em dashes" (footnote 2). The agent also used non-ASCII characters, including U+2011 non-breaking hyphens and emojis/nonstandard bullets that render poorly on some platforms.
- Deliverable text accompanying the file was frequently verbose, sometimes contained links to the submitted files, and sometimes attempted to deliver content inline in the text rather than in a file.
- PDFs were generated via non-LibreOffice toolchains.

## 3. Signals / feedback received
- The agent's harness gave it **no automated visual feedback loop**: the agent did not, on its own, convert the deliverable to images and look at the rendered output before submission.
- Internet GET requests were initially restricted in the container (the paper notes "enabling GET requests in the container" as a *later* scaffolding improvement, implying they weren't enabled initially).
- The only feedback that reached the agent during a run was whatever the model elicited itself (e.g., reading its own code interpreter outputs); end-of-task expert grading happened externally and didn't feed back into the agent.

## 4. Where things went wrong (observed defects in deliverables)
When industry-expert graders compared GPT-5 high outputs to human deliverables (Figure 8 clustering pipeline, Section 3.3), GPT-5 had the *fewest* instruction-following accuracy errors among models but the *most* losses attributable to **formatting** problems. Concretely:

- **Black-square artifacts** appeared in **more than half** of the PDFs the agent produced.
- **Egregious formatting errors** appeared in **86%** of the PowerPoint files the agent produced (text/graphics cut off the page, overlapping elements, blank pages, illegible/dark-on-dark or light-on-light text, etc.).
- Non-portable characters (U+2011 hyphens, emojis, nonstandard bullets) rendered poorly on grader machines.
- Embedded fonts were not always cross-platform.
- Deliverable text was over-verbose and sometimes linked to or duplicated the file content.
- Many deliverables were submitted without the agent ever opening/viewing the rendered output (the 15% inspection rate).
- Section 3.3 / Appendix A.2.6 reports the severity breakdown: the most common category of GPT-5 failure was "acceptable but subpar"; roughly **29%** of failures were "bad or catastrophic" (about **3%** catastrophic — e.g., dangerously wrong outputs in domains like medicine).

## 5. The intervention (Section 3.4 + Appendix A.3)
OpenAI then ran a second experiment to test whether prompting and scaffolding could mitigate these defects:

- **Prompt-tuning (Appendix A.3, full text reproduced in the paper).** The new system prompt told the agent to:
  - Use U+002D, never U+2011; avoid emojis/nonstandard bullets/special characters.
  - Make embedded plots ≥ half-page-width; avoid overlay-of-shapes "complicated visuals."
  - Build PDFs **only** with LibreOffice, installing it if missing; use Noto Sans/Serif or embed any other font.
  - Keep deliverable text ≤ 4 sentences, no links to files, put deliverables in files (not in text), call out unsolvable portions.
  - Default to "standard" filetypes (PDF/PPTX/DOCX/XLSX/MP4/ZIP) when unspecified; extract frames from MP4/MOV and check them.
  - Perform **mandatory formatting checks** before submission: (1) convert every visual deliverable to per-page PNGs via LibreOffice; (2) actually display the PNGs and look for cut-off / overlapping / blank / illegible content; (3) write programmatic checks for blank pages, overflow, overlaps, page-limit violations; (4) restate prompt requirements and match them to the deliverable; (5) re-open every file right before submitting. Loop until clean. Append `CONFIDENCE[XX]` on the last line.
- **Scaffolding changes.** GET requests were enabled in the container, and **best-of-N sampling with N=4 plus a GPT-5 judge** picked the final submission.

## 6. Final outcome reported
- **Black-square PDF artifacts**: from >50% of PDFs → **fully eliminated**.
- **Egregious PowerPoint formatting errors**: **86% → 64%**.
- **Agents using multi-modal capabilities to inspect their own deliverables**: **15% → 97%**.
- **Human-expert preference win rate** for GPT-5: improved by **~5 percentage points** (Figure 9b).
- Increasing reasoning effort (low → medium → high) on o3 and GPT-5 also produced monotonically higher win rates (Figure 9a).
- Even after the intervention, formatting errors remained the dominant residual failure mode, and overall GPT-5 win rates against human experts on the gold subset remained below those of Claude Opus 4.1, which the paper attributes to Claude's stronger aesthetics/layout handling.

Sources:
- [GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks (arXiv:2510.04374)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04374) — Sections 3.3, 3.4, A.2.6, and A.3 in particular.

# Chronological account of the GPT-5 (high reasoning) agent's behaviour on GDPval

## 1. Task and setup
- The agent was given GDPval gold-subset prompts: real-world, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks contributed by industry experts across 9 sectors and 44 occupations. Each prompt typically includes a written request plus up to 17 reference files (spreadsheets, slide decks, PDFs, images, audio, video, CAD, etc.) and asks for a deliverable file (often PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, or ZIP). Average expert completion time is ~7 hours; some tasks span weeks.
- The agent was GPT-5 at *high* reasoning effort, running in OpenAI's custom GDPval harness with the **web search** and **code interpreter** tools enabled, in background-sampling mode. Several non-default libraries were preinstalled in the container. Each prompt was sampled three times for the headline run.

## 2. Steps and tool calls observed in the baseline (pre-mitigation) runs
The paper reports the following observable behaviours of the unprompted agent across the gold subset (Section 3.3 and the opening of Section 3.4):

- The agent read the prompt + reference files, used web search and code interpreter, and then generated deliverable files (PDFs, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, etc.) inside the container.
- For multimodal deliverables, the agent typically **did not** use its multi-modal capabilities to render or inspect what it had just produced before submitting. The paper reports the rate of agents "using their multi-modal capabilities to inspect deliverables" at only **15%** prior to the prompt change.
- Stylistic tells noted by graders: outputs "often used em dashes" (footnote 2). The agent also used non-ASCII characters, including U+2011 non-breaking hyphens and emojis/nonstandard bullets that render poorly on some platforms.
- Deliverable text accompanying the file was frequently verbose, sometimes contained links to the submitted files, and sometimes attempted to deliver content inline in the text rather than in a file.
- PDFs were generated via non-LibreOffice toolchains.

## 3. Signals / feedback received
- The agent's harness gave it **no automated visual feedback loop**: the agent did not, on its own, convert the deliverable to images and look at the rendered output before submission.
- Internet GET requests were initially restricted in the container (the paper notes "enabling GET requests in the container" as a *later* scaffolding improvement, implying they weren't enabled initially).
- The only feedback that reached the agent during a run was whatever the model elicited itself (e.g., reading its own code interpreter outputs); end-of-task expert grading happened externally and didn't feed back into the agent.

## 4. Where things went wrong (observed defects in deliverables)
When industry-expert graders compared GPT-5 high outputs to human deliverables (Figure 8 clustering pipeline, Section 3.3), GPT-5 had the *fewest* instruction-following accuracy errors among models but the *most* losses attributable to **formatting** problems. Concretely:

- **Black-square artifacts** appeared in **more than half** of the PDFs the agent produced.
- **Egregious formatting errors** appeared in **86%** of the PowerPoint files the agent produced (text/graphics cut off the page, overlapping elements, blank pages, illegible/dark-on-dark or light-on-light text, etc.).
- Non-portable characters (U+2011 hyphens, emojis, nonstandard bullets) rendered poorly on grader machines.
